paper_title: A new model for learning in graph domains
abstract: This paper presents a new neural model, called graph neural network (GNN), capable of directly processing graphs. GNNs extends recursive neural networks and can be applied to cyclic graphs. The model learns to encode the entire graph structure and node features into a distributed representation, enabling processing of graph-structured data in domains where the relationships between entities are important.
key_contributions: Introduced the first Graph Neural Network (GNN) model capable of processing graph-structured data directly
Extended recursive neural networks to handle cyclic graphs through a contraction process
Developed a learning algorithm based on gradient descent that converges to a fixed point
Demonstrated applications in graph processing tasks including web page ranking and molecular property prediction
relevance_to_cross_residual_gnn: Foundational paper that introduced the concept of learning directly on graph-structured data. The contraction process and state-based representation are early precursors to modern graph representation learning. The residual connections in ECR-GNN build upon this foundation by enabling deeper architectures.

paper_title: Semi-supervised classification with graph convolutional networks
abstract: We present a scalable approach for semi-supervised learning on graph-structured data that is based on an efficient variant of convolutional neural networks which operate directly on graphs. We motivate the choice of our convolutional architecture via a localized first-order approximation of spectral graph convolutions. Our model scales linearly in the number of graph edges and learns hidden layer representations that encode both local graph structure and features of nodes. In a number of experiments on citation networks and on a knowledge graph dataset we demonstrate that our approach outperforms related methods by a significant margin.
key_contributions: Introduced Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) with first-order approximation of spectral convolutions
Developed a scalable, layer-wise propagation rule for semi-supervised node classification
Achieved linear computational complexity in the number of edges
Demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on citation network benchmarks (Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed)
methods: Spectral graph convolutions with first-order approximation
Neighbor aggregation with normalized adjacency matrix
relevance_to_cross_residual_gnn: This is the foundational GCN paper that ECR-GNN builds upon. The GCN layer is the base convolution operation used in ECR-GNN. The cross-layer residual connections directly address the limitation that GCNs cannot be stacked deeply due to over-smoothing.

paper_title: Inductive representation learning on large graphs
venue: Advances in neural information processing systems
abstract: Low-dimensional embeddings of nodes in large graphs have proved extremely useful in a variety of prediction tasks, from content recommendation to identifying protein functions. However, most existing approaches require that all nodes in the graph are present during training and cannot naturally generalize to unseen nodes. Here we present GraphSAGE, a general, inductive framework that leverages node feature information (e.g., text attributes) to efficiently generate node embeddings for previously unseen data. Instead of training individual embeddings for each node, we learn a function that generates embeddings by sampling and aggregating features from a node's local neighborhood.
key_contributions: Introduced GraphSAGE, an inductive framework for node embedding that generalizes to unseen nodes
Developed neighborhood sampling and aggregation functions for efficient learning
Demonstrated three aggregation architectures: mean aggregator, LSTM aggregator, and pooling aggregator
Achieved state-of-the-art results on three inductive node classification benchmarks
relevance_to_cross_residual_gnn: GraphSAGE's aggregation functions and inductive capabilities are relevant to ECR-GNN's design. The multi-scale aggregation in ECR-GNN could incorporate similar aggregation strategies across different layers.

paper_title: Graph attention networks
abstract: We present graph attention networks (GATs), novel neural network architectures that operate on graph-structured data, leveraging masked self-attentional layers to address the shortcomings of prior methods based on graph convolutions or their approximations. By stacking layers in which nodes are able to attend over their neighborhoods' features, we enable (implicitly) specifying different weights to different nodes in a neighborhood, without requiring any kind of costly matrix operation (such as inversion) or depending on knowing the graph structure upfront. In this way, we address several key challenges of spectral-based graph neural networks simultaneously, and make our model readily applicable to inductive as well as transductive problems.
key_contributions: Introduced Graph Attention Networks (GAT) using self-attention mechanisms for graph data
Enabled nodes to attend to different neighbors with different weights
Achieved inductive learning without requiring graph structure upfront
Demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on Cora, Citeseer, Pubmed, and protein-protein interaction datasets
relevance_to_cross_residual_gnn: GAT's attention mechanism for weighting neighbor contributions is highly relevant to ECR-GNN. The adaptive readout function in ECR-GNN could incorporate similar attention mechanisms to weight contributions from different layers.

paper_title: How powerful are graph neural networks?
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are an effective framework for representation learning of graphs. GNNs follow a neighborhood aggregation scheme, where the representation vector of a node is computed by recursively aggregating and transforming representation vectors of its neighboring nodes. Many GNN variants have been proposed and have achieved state-of-the-art results on both node and graph classification tasks. However, despite GNNs revolutionizing graph representation learning, there is limited understanding of their representational properties and limitations. Here, we present a theoretical framework for analyzing the expressive power of GNNs to capture different graph structures. Our results characterize the discriminative power of popular GNN variants, such as Graph Convolutional Networks and GraphSAGE, and show that they cannot learn to distinguish certain simple graph structures. We then develop a simple architecture that is provably the most expressive among the class of GNNs and is as powerful as the Weisfeiler-Lehman graph isomorphism test.
key_contributions: Developed a theoretical framework for analyzing the expressive power of GNNs
Showed that GCN and GraphSAGE cannot distinguish certain simple graph structures
Introduced Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN), provably as powerful as the Weisfeiler-Lehman test
Demonstrated that GIN achieves state-of-the-art performance on graph classification benchmarks
methods: Theoretical analysis of GNN expressive power
relevance_to_cross_residual_gnn: This paper's theoretical analysis of GNN expressive power is fundamental. ECR-GNN's cross-layer connections help maintain discriminative power in deep networks, addressing some limitations identified in this work.

paper_title: Convolutional networks on graphs for learning molecular fingerprints
venue: Advances in neural information processing systems
abstract: We introduce a convolutional neural network that operates directly on graphs. These networks allow end-to-end learning of prediction pipelines whose inputs are graphs and whose outputs are properties of interest. In the chemistry domain, these networks learn to predict molecular properties directly from the molecular graph structure. Our architecture generalizes standard molecular feature extraction methods based on circular fingerprints.
key_contributions: Introduced convolutional neural networks that operate directly on graph structures
Developed an architecture for learning molecular fingerprints end-to-end
Generalized circular fingerprint methods with learnable parameters
Demonstrated improved molecular property prediction on benchmark datasets
relevance_to_cross_residual_gnn: This early work on graph convolutions for molecular fingerprints demonstrates the value of learning representations directly from graph structure. ECR-GNN applies similar principles to graph classification tasks.

paper_title: Neural message passing for quantum chemistry
abstract: In this paper, we reformulate existing models into a single common framework we call Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) and explore additional novel variants within this framework. MPNNs are a class of graph neural networks that operate on graph-structured data, where information is propagated between nodes through message passing operations. We demonstrate that MPNNs achieve state-of-the-art results on an important molecular property prediction benchmark, predicting DFT to within chemical accuracy on 11 out of 13 targets.
key_contributions: Unified existing graph neural network models into the Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) framework
Identified two key functions: message function and vertex update function
Achieved state-of-the-art results on quantum chemistry benchmarks
Demonstrated the power of message passing for molecular property prediction
methods: Message passing and vertex update functions
relevance_to_cross_residual_gnn: The MPNN framework provides a unified view of graph neural networks that ECR-GNN falls under. The message passing paradigm is the foundation for information propagation in ECR-GNN's layers.

paper_title: Hierarchical graph representation learning with differentiable pooling
venue: Advances in neural information processing systems
abstract: Recently, graph neural networks (GNNs) have revolutionized the field of graph representation learning through effectively learned node embeddings, and achieved state-of-the-art results in tasks such as node classification and link prediction. However, current GNN methods are inherently flat and do not learn hierarchical representations of graphs---a limitation that is especially problematic for the task of graph classification, where the goal is to predict the label associated with an entire graph. Here we propose DiffPool, a differentiable graph pooling module that can generate hierarchical representations of graphs and can be combined with various graph neural network architectures in an end-to-end fashion. DiffPool learns a differentiable soft cluster assignment for nodes at each layer of a deep GNN, mapping nodes to a set of clusters, which then form the coarsened input for the next GNN layer.
key_contributions: Introduced DiffPool, a differentiable graph pooling module for hierarchical graph representation learning
Enabled end-to-end learning of node cluster assignments
Addressed the limitation that GNNs are inherently flat and don't learn hierarchical representations
Achieved 5-10% improvement on graph classification benchmarks over existing pooling approaches
methods: Graph pooling with soft cluster assignments
relevance_to_cross_residual_gnn: DiffPool's hierarchical approach is directly relevant to ECR-GNN. While DiffPool uses pooling to create hierarchies, ECR-GNN uses cross-layer connections to maintain multi-scale information without discarding nodes.

paper_title: Self-attention graph pooling
abstract: Advanced methods of applying deep learning to structured data such as graphs have been proposed in recent years. In particular, studies have focused on generalizing convolutional neural networks to graph data, which includes redefining the convolution and the downsampling (pooling) operations for graphs. The method of generalizing the convolution operation to graphs has been proven to improve performance and is widely used. However, the method of applying downsampling to graphs is still difficult to perform and has room for improvement. In this paper, we propose a graph pooling method based on self-attention. Self-attention using graph convolution allows our pooling method to consider both node features and graph topology. To ensure a fair comparison, the same training procedures and model architectures were used for the existing pooling methods and our method.
key_contributions: Introduced SAGPool, a self-attention based graph pooling method
Used graph convolution to compute attention scores for node selection
Enabled pooling that considers both node features and graph topology
Achieved superior graph classification performance on benchmark datasets
relevance_to_cross_residual_gnn: SAGPool's use of attention to weight node importance is relevant to ECR-GNN's adaptive readout function. Both approaches use learnable attention mechanisms to determine the importance of different components.

paper_title: Towards sparse hierarchical graph classifiers
venue: Pacific-Asia Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
abstract: Here we combine several recent advances in graph neural network design to demonstrate that competitive hierarchical graph classification results are possible with much simpler architectures than previously proposed. We introduce a learnable graph local pooling method, termed LocalPool, which first employs graph neural network operations to learn the importance of each node and then selects the most important nodes to form a coarsened graph. The method is sparse, differentiable, and can be trained end-to-end.
key_contributions: Introduced LocalPool, a sparse and differentiable graph pooling method
Combined multiple advances in GNN design for hierarchical graph classification
Demonstrated competitive results with simpler architectures
Enabled end-to-end training with learnable node importance
relevance_to_cross_residual_gnn: This work on sparse hierarchical classifiers is relevant to ECR-GNN's approach to maintaining information across layers. ECR-GNN avoids sparsity by using cross-layer connections to preserve information.

paper_title: Graph neural networks with convolutional ARMA filters
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Popular graph neural networks implement convolution operations on graphs based on polynomial spectral filters. In this paper, we propose a novel graph convolutional layer inspired by the auto-regressive moving average (ARMA) filter that, compared to polynomial ones, provides a more flexible frequency response, is more robust to noise, and better captures the global graph structure. We propose a graph neural network implementation of the ARMA filter with a recursive and distributed formulation, obtaining a convolutional layer that is efficient to train, localized in the node space, and can be transferred to new graphs at test time.
key_contributions: Introduced ARMA filters for graph convolution, providing more flexible frequency response than polynomial filters
Developed recursive and distributed formulation for efficient training
Demonstrated better robustness to noise and global structure capture
Achieved significant improvements over polynomial filter-based GNNs on four downstream tasks
relevance_to_cross_residual_gnn: The ARMA filter approach offers an alternative to standard GCN layers that ECR-GNN could use as base convolutions. The recursive formulation relates to the cross-layer connections in ECR-GNN.

paper_title: Deeper insights into graph convolutional networks for semi-supervised learning
abstract: This paper provides deeper insights into graph convolutional networks (GCNs) for semi-supervised learning. The authors analyze the limitations of GCNs and propose improvements to enable deeper architectures.
key_contributions: Analyzed limitations of standard GCNs in deep architectures
Identified over-smoothing as a key problem in deep GCNs
Proposed techniques to enable deeper GCN architectures

venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
abstract: This paper proposes conditional graph convolutions for predicting drug-protein binding. The method conditions the convolution operation on specific graph properties to improve prediction accuracy.

paper_title: Deep residual learning for image recognition
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE conference on computer vision and pattern recognition
abstract: Deeper neural networks are more difficult to train. We present a residual learning framework to ease the training of networks that are substantially deeper than those used previously. We explicitly reformulate the layers as learning residual functions with reference to the layer inputs, instead of learning unreferenced functions. We provide comprehensive empirical evidence showing that these residual networks are easier to optimize, and can gain accuracy from considerably increased depth.
key_contributions: Introduced ResNet, a residual learning framework for deep networks
Demonstrated that residual connections enable training of very deep networks (152 layers)
Won 1st place in ILSVRC 2015 classification task
Showed 28% relative improvement on COCO object detection
relevance_to_cross_residual_gnn: This is the foundational ResNet paper that inspired residual connections in all domains. ECR-GNN's cross-layer residual connections are directly inspired by and adapted from this work for graph data.

paper_title: Representation learning on graphs with jumping knowledge networks
abstract: Recent deep learning approaches for representation learning on graphs follow a neighborhood aggregation procedure. We analyze some important properties of these models, and propose a strategy to overcome those. In particular, the range of "neighboring" nodes that a node's representation draws from strongly depends on the graph structure, analogous to the spread of a random walk. To adapt to local neighborhood properties and tasks, we explore an architecture -- jumping knowledge (JK) networks -- that flexibly leverages, for each node, different neighborhood ranges to enable better structure-aware representation.
key_contributions: Introduced Jumping Knowledge (JK) networks for flexible neighborhood range selection
Enabled adaptive aggregation from different layers
Demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on social, bioinformatics, and citation networks
Showed consistent improvement when combining JK with GCN, GraphSAGE, and GAT
relevance_to_cross_residual_gnn: JK networks are highly relevant to ECR-GNN's multi-scale aggregation. Both approaches leverage information from multiple layers, with ECR-GNN using cross-layer connections similar to JK's layer combination.

paper_title: Combining label propagation and simple models out-performs graph neural networks
abstract: Neural message passing algorithms for semi-supervised classification on graphs have recently achieved great success. However, for classifying a node these methods only consider nodes that are a few propagation steps away and the size of this utilized neighborhood is hard to extend. In this paper, we use the relationship between graph convolutional networks (GCN) and PageRank to derive an improved propagation scheme based on personalized PageRank. We utilize this propagation procedure to construct a simple model, personalized propagation of neural predictions (PPNP), and its fast approximation, APPNP.
key_contributions: Derived relationship between GCN and PageRank
Introduced PPNP and APPNP using personalized PageRank propagation
Enabled utilization of large, adjustable neighborhoods
Achieved state-of-the-art results with fewer parameters and faster training
relevance_to_cross_residual_gnn: The PageRank-based propagation offers an alternative to standard GCN layers. ECR-GNN could incorporate such propagation schemes within its cross-layer framework.
